newsitem.title: UK: Britain's Major rejects EU deal on fishing cuts.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Major rejects EU deal on fishing cuts.

text.p: Britain will not implement a European Union deal to cut fishing quotas by up to 30 percent until the EU solves the problem of so-called "quota hoppers", Prime Minister John Major said on Tuesday.
"I have not a shred of intention of cutting the British catch until or unless we get a satisfactory agreement on quota hopping," Major told reporters.

Major, campaigning ahead of nationwide elections on May 1, was speaking during a visit to the cattle market in Tavistock, western England, after EU fisheries ministers agreed on the cutbacks as part of measures to conserve stocks.
Seeking fishermen's votes, Major has adopted a tough line on the fisheries issue, which reflects an emergent mood of anti-European feeling in his ruling Conservative Party.
He repeated a threat he made on Monday that Britain would block the conclusion of June's Amsterdam summit on the future shape of the EU unless the problem of quota hopping was tackled.

Quota hopping refers to the perfectly legal practice whereby foreign fishermen, mainly Spanish and Dutch, have bought up about 25 percent of the British fishing fleet to gain greater access to EU catch quotas.
Britain, supported only by France, was outvoted on Tuesday when EU fisheries ministers meeting in Luxembourg decided on the 30 percent cuts in catches.
Britain believes it can meet the 30 percent target by eliminating quota-hoppers.
Major said the Luxembourg setback underlined the importance of not surrendering Britain's veto in any other areas of European policy.
"If it illustrates one thing very clearly, it illustrates why I am resolutely opposed towards even more matters being decided by qualified majority vote.

"It illustrates why I very strongly oppose the concept of a federal Europe and it illustrates why I believe the Labour Party and the Liberal Democrats are utterly wrong to suggest they will sacrifice the veto in large areas of great national concern."
The main opposition Labour Party, which has moved closer to the Conservatives on a range of issues, has also promised to use the veto in EU business if Britain's interests are threatened.
But Labour economics spokesman Gordon Brown said the government's failure to get a decent deal for British fishermen was the latest in a long line of EU negotiating rebuffs.
"It seems to be very much a re-run of the beef issue," Brown told a news conference in London, referring to the EU ban on exports of British beef because of the mad cow crisis.
Labour leader Tony Blair said on Monday: "Where Britain's interests are at stake, we are perfectly prepared to be isolated. What we don't seek is a policy of perpetual isolation."
